result:
I'll write about something that's been on my mind lately: the strange intimacy of strangers.

---

There's a particular kind of loneliness that doesn't come from being alone, but from being surrounded by people you will never know. I think about this most often on subways, where bodies press together in temporary, anonymous congress. The woman reading a water-damaged paperback, its pages swollen with humidity. The teenager whose headphones leak tinny percussion. The man with grocery bags looped around his wrists like oversized bracelets, onions and cilantro visible through thin plastic. Each of them contains an entire universe—childhood fears, favorite songs, the specific way they take their coffee, whether they believe in anything after death—and we are compressed together for four stops, maybe six, sharing nothing but the recycled air and the slight vibration of wheels on track.

I used to find this unbearable. Now I think it might be the most honest thing about city life.

We carry this fiction that human connection requires depth, that knowing someone means excavating their history, learning their wounds, becoming keeper of their secrets. But I've started to wonder if there's something equally human in the shallow encounter, the unreciprocated observation, the momentary recognition of another person's existence without any demand for reciprocity. The barista who remembers your order but not your name. The neighbor whose schedule you know by the sound of their door. These are incomplete relationships, yes, but they're not failed ones. They're a different species entirely.

Last month I watched an elderly man at a bus stop in the rain. He had one of those compact umbrellas that barely covered his shoulders, and he kept tilting it this way and that, trying to find an angle that would keep both his head and his paper grocery bag dry. It was futile, obviously. The bag was already darkening with water, its structural integrity failing in real time. He knew it too; I could see that in the particular set of his jaw, the way he wasn't really trying to solve the problem so much as perform the effort of caring. For whose benefit? Maybe his own. Maybe mine, though we hadn't exchanged a glance. I wanted to offer him my umbrella—larger, useless to me in the coffee shop I was headed to—but the bus arrived before I could overcome the vast gulf of stranger-protocol, that invisible force field that keeps us in our orbits.

I still think about that bag. Whether the bread inside survived. Whether he told anyone about his soggy walk home, or if it simply dissolved into the general texture of his day, unremarked and unremarkable.

This is what I mean by intimacy. Not the grand gestures, the sworn devotion, the midnight confessions. The smaller thing: having witnessed someone in their small, private futility. The umbrella man doesn't know I carry him. I am, for him, nothing. But for me, he exists in a particular way that he doesn't for the other twenty people at that stop, most of whom were looking at phones, who have already forgotten the rain entirely.

There's a Japanese concept, *mono no aware*, often translated as "the pathos of things"—the bittersweet awareness of impermanence. Cherry blossoms are the classic example, their beauty intensified by their briefness. I think the bus stop man is my cherry blossom. The woman on the train with her swollen book. All these people I will never speak to, who nevertheless leave their fingerprints on my consciousness, however faintly.

It makes me wonder about my own anonymity in other lives. How many times have I been someone's fleeting observation? The woman crying in a parking garage (last Tuesday, work thing, nothing serious but everything urgent in the moment). The person who dropped an orange at the grocery store and watched it roll under the lettuce display, too embarrassed to retrieve it. Someone, somewhere, might remember me only as a silhouette in a window, a voice overheard saying something inexplicable out of context. "But that's not even a real dinosaur," I apparently said on a phone call once, walking past a couple on the street. I saw them laugh, saw them turn to each other with that particular look—*did you hear that?*—and I kept walking, already moving out of their story, becoming a punchline they'd forget by dinner, if they even made it that far.

I find this comforting rather than sad. There's a democracy to it. We are all, simultaneously, protagonists and extras, deeply known to a few and barely noticed by hundreds, thousands, millions. The scale of our unknownness is vast, almost cosmic, and there's relief in that. The pressure to be fully seen, completely understood, to have our entire selves metabolized by another person—that's crushing, impossible, maybe undesirable. The strangers offer an alternative. They see only what we present in a given moment, without the weight of context, without the burden of reconciliation. They receive us as pure surface, and sometimes surface is exactly what we need to be.

I'm not arguing against real friendship, against love, against the slow work of being known. Those remain the great projects of a life. But I want to make room for this other thing, these glancing connections that don't accumulate into anything but still matter in their passing. The nurse who chatted with me while drawing blood, who I'll never see again but who made that particular morning bearable. The child who waved at me from a car window, performing friendliness before they learned to be selective. The dog walker who nodded once, acknowledging our shared presence in the early dark, two people awake before the world required it.

Maybe this is all a way of saying that I believe in a kind of distributed humanity. We don't need to know each other to be, briefly, together. The subway car is a community of non-community, a solidarity of solitude. Everyone in it is equally unknown, equally present, equally on their way somewhere else. There's something almost spiritual in that, if I can use that word without believing in much spiritually. The temporary congregation. The unspoken contract: I will not demand anything of you, and in exchange, I will let you exist in your full complexity without reducing you to your utility in my story.

The umbrella man is still walking home in my mind, still failing to keep his groceries dry. The woman with the swollen book has finished it by now, probably, or abandoned it, or started it again from the beginning because she wasn't paying attention the first time. I hope the teenager found better headphones. I hope the cilantro became something good. I hope they were all, in their own ways, as seen as they needed to be—not by me, not specifically, but by the general fact of sharing space with other humans who are also trying, also failing in small ways, also carrying their own invisible weather.

That's enough. That's the thousand words, and maybe more than I intended to say about people I'll never meet. But that's the point, isn't it? The saying without the needing-to-be-heard. The writing without knowing who reads. The bus stop in the rain, where we stand together, separately, before the next thing arrives to carry us away.
